newsitem.title: USA: A hotel chain goes after big names with low prices.
newsitem.headline: A hotel chain goes after big names with low prices.

text.p: Watch it, Ritz-Carlton Hotels. Intercontinental Hotels. Fairfield. Holiday Inns. Days Inns. There's a powerhouse chain with about 240 limited-service hotels that's about to breathe down your neck.

La Quinta Inns, based in San Antonio, has an average room rate of about $52 but is pitching upscale, comfort and service that will probably give it high exposure to travelers who usually stay at the full-service establishments and charge three to five times as much -- and it has no intention of raising its room rates.

Now is the time to make a push, with industry conditions better than they've been in over a decade: The full-service hotels are operating at capacity on weekdays and are turning away prospective guests. In general, the lodging industry is facing a tightening supply/demand situation. Last year, occupancy rose to 65.7 percent, the highest level in 15 years.

La Quinta's rate has risen to almost 70 percent this year. Unlike many of the other hotel chains that consist of largely franchised units, La Quinta owns all its own hotels, consisting of a total 30,000 rooms, which gives it tighter quality control than it would have if it were franchised.
And that is the thrust of the company's marketing push, centred on the theme, "Make Yourself at Home," which has drawn new attention to it and attracted favourable interest from Wall Street.

"By providing this high-value guest experience, La Quinta will be well positioned to attract travelers who typically stay at full-service hotels," said Camille E. Humphries, industry analyst for Alex Brown & Sons.

The upgrade package includes improved bathrooms with better lighting, built-in closets and new carpets, bedspreads and wall coverings, video and movies on demand, 22 channels of cable TV, computer modems in all the guest rooms and an expanded, complimentary breakfast offering, Humphries noted.
"This is an important strategic initiative, which will strengthen the company's long-term competitive position," she said.

New management was brought in after Lee and Sid Bass and Thomas Taylor led a dissident investor group that acquired 15 percent of the company in 1992. They pushed for a restructuring, which in turn touched off the new, upscale marketing campaign.

"Our marketing-and-advertising theme, 'Make Yourself at Home, is aimed at telling the travelling public that our rooms are much more residential and comfortable than other limited-service hotels," said Chris Trick, La Quinta's national marketing manager.

"Certainly, we are trying to improve our market share but we really sort of compare ourselves with ourselves. That may have helped us push our occupancy rate to almost 70 percent. We are considered a mid-market brand in rates but also an upper-economy hotel in service. That makes us different, I believe."
The company's advertising agency is Publicis/Bloom, in Dallas.

In the view of Humphries of Alex Brown, La Quinta has one of the best management teams in the lodging industry. Gary Mead, the chief executive, and other senior managers have strong experience in the lodging business, particularly with Motel 6, Embassy Suites and Holiday Inns.
Already the nation's largest owner-operator of hotels (most of the big chains are substantially franchised), La Quinta expects to add between 18 and 24 new hotels a year.
With companies like La Quinta in mind, another analyst points to rising competition from limited-service hotels, especially those that are expanding.
"To most travelers, either for pleasure or business, the price point is the key differentiation," observes Michael J. Rietbrock of Smith Barney Inc., New York.

The full service hotels, he said, could be vulnerable to the likes of La Quinta, even if they appear invulnerable in the current robust environment. "There may only seem to be a protective wall around full-service hotels, especially in non-urban, less-than-luxury locations, from the development of new limited-service product."
